subject: physics
title: Maximum Height of a Thrown Ball
problem: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of $20\text{ m/s}$. Assuming the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ and ignoring air resistance, what is the maximum height reached by the ball?
solution_steps: Identify the known variables: initial velocity $v_i = 20\text{ m/s}$, final velocity at maximum height $v_f = 0\text{ m/s}$, and acceleration $a = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
Select the kinematic equation that relates these variables: $v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2a\Delta y$.
Substitute the known values into the equation: $0^2 = 20^2 + 2(-9.8)\Delta y$.
Solve for the displacement $\Delta y$: $0 = 400 - 19.6\Delta y$, which yields $\Delta y = \frac{400}{19.6} \approx 20.4\text{ m}$.
common_mistake: Forgetting that the acceleration due to gravity acts in the opposite direction of the initial upward velocity, leading to sign errors in the kinematic equation.

subject: physics
title: Acceleration of a Pulled Block
problem: A $2\text{ kg}$ block on a frictionless horizontal table is pulled by a constant horizontal force of $10\text{ N}$. Find the acceleration of the block.
solution_steps: Identify the given values: mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ and net horizontal force $F = 10\text{ N}$.
Use Newton's second law of motion, $F = ma$, and rearrange it to solve for acceleration: $a = \frac{F}{m}$.
Substitute the values into the formula: $a = \frac{10\text{ N}}{2\text{ kg}} = 5\text{ m/s}^2$.
common_mistake: Multiplying the force by the mass ($a = F \cdot m$) instead of dividing, resulting in an incorrect acceleration of $20\text{ m/s}^2$.
